messages.content: My program doesn't work.
Let's narrow it down. What does 'doesn't work' mean here: does it crash, produce the wrong output, freeze, or do nothing? The exact behavior will tell us where to start.
The program crashes.
Good, that gives us something concrete. Get the full error message and traceback first. Then we can identify the exact line that failed.
The error says a variable doesn't exist.
Check where that variable is created and whether that code runs before the failing line. Also check spelling and scope. A NameError is often caused by one of those.
My model gives garbage output.

First determine whether the model is trained at all. Then check the tokenizer, checkpoint loading, input formatting, model dtype, and generation code. Garbage output can come from several different layers.
My training loss is not changing.

Check whether the optimizer is actually stepping, whether gradients are nonzero, whether the learning rate is reasonable, and whether the same data is being repeated unexpectedly. Don't assume the model architecture is the problem.
My training is extremely slow.
Measure where the time goes first. Check data loading, CPU usage, GPU utilization, memory transfers, sequence length, batch size, and whether the model is actually running on the GPU.
My GPU isn't being used.
Check torch.cuda.is_available(), the selected device, the model's device, and the tensors' devices. A CUDA-capable GPU existing in the computer doesn't automatically mean the model is using it.
My code used to work.
Then look for the smallest change between the working and broken versions. A regression is often easier to solve by comparing changes than by rewriting everything.
I changed ten things and now it broke.
That's harder to debug because there are ten possible causes. Revert or isolate the changes, then introduce them one at a time until the failure appears.
Should I rewrite everything?
Usually not as a first step. Identify the actual failure first. Rewriting can remove the bug, but it can also create ten new ones.
An AI-generated script invented an API route.
Don't assume the route exists. Check the actual backend source and route definitions. If the route isn't there, either use an existing route or explicitly add the new route.
An AI-generated script changed my database column names.
Compare the script against the actual database schema. Database names should not be changed just because generated code uses different names. Compatibility comes first.
I don't know where the bug is.
Then don't guess randomly. Reproduce the bug, collect the error or incorrect output, and narrow the problem down layer by layer.
There are three possible causes.
Test them one at a time. Start with the easiest hypothesis to verify or the one most strongly supported by the evidence.
The fix didn't work.
Then the original hypothesis may have been wrong or incomplete. Keep the evidence, undo unnecessary changes, and test the next likely cause.
I think I know the problem.
Great. State the hypothesis and what evidence supports it. Then we can test it instead of treating it as fact.
What if there isn't enough information?
Then say what's missing. A good diagnosis should distinguish between what is known, what is likely, and what is still unknown.
